hackneyed

HAK-need · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Hackneyed is unoriginal because it has been used too often.

The critic dismissed the film's ending as a hackneyed twist audiences had seen a hundred times before.

Example

The commencement speech leaned on so many hackneyed phrases about "following your dreams" that half the graduates stopped listening.

Hackneyed describes a phrase, plot, or idea that has been repeated so many times it no longer feels fresh or interesting.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

clichéd: A clichéd line leans on a specific stock formula everyone can finish — 'happily ever after,' 'only time will tell.' Hackneyed is the broader judgment: hackneyed language or ideas of any shape have been repeated so often that all the freshness has been worn out of them.

trite: Trite describes a remark or idea that has gone flat and shallow from overuse, so it lands with no weight at all. Hackneyed points at the wear itself: a hackneyed phrase has simply been handled too many times, like a coin rubbed smooth.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

original: new and not copied from anything else

fresh: new and interesting

Where it sits · how worn out from overuse — familiar → hackneyed → stale

familiar vs. hackneyed: Something familiar is merely well-known, which is far milder than hackneyed: a favorite old joke everyone knows can still get a laugh, while a hackneyed one has been told so often it only gets groans.

stale vs. hackneyed: Something stale has gone completely flat and lifeless, an even harsher judgment than merely hackneyed.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — hackney

root — hackney: a horse for ordinary riding or hire (Middle English, possibly from the London district Hackney)

suffix — -ed

suffix — -ed: having the quality of (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: hackney ("a horse for hire") + -ed = worn out from constant, ordinary use.

Use the root in a new word: hackney carriage

Use the root in a new word: hackney carriage: A "hackney" was originally an ordinary horse rented out for everyday riding -- used so constantly and unremarkably that "hackneyed" came to mean worn out and unoriginal. London's licensed taxis are still officially called "hackney carriages" today.

Word Building

Word Choice

Hackneyed describes language or ideas -- a phrase, plot, or expression worn out from overuse -- rather than physical decay or a rigid attitude, which is what "putrefy" and "hidebound" describe.
